_meta.id_conventions: S = source, F = fact, X = comparable, C = claim, Q = open question
rules: Every fact needs a source with URL and access date before status can be 'verified'.
PPP for all cross-country income/productivity comparisons, never nominal exchange rates.
When two reputable sources disagree, record both and set status to 'challenged'.
Never delete a refuted fact; keep it with its refutation so no future run re-adds it.
Set chartable: true on facts carrying data series worth charting in the future HTML rendering.

facts.statement: French general government expenditure was 57.0% of GDP in 2024 and 58.2% in 2025, among the highest in the OECD (OECD average: 42.6% in 2023). Only Finland is comparable (57.5% in 2024).
facts.notes: INSEE and OECD figures differ by ~0.2pp (57.0 vs 57.2 for 2024) due to vintage; immaterial. Time series in S001 goes back to 2018.

facts.statement: French public debt (Maastricht definition) was 112.6% of GDP in 2024 and 115.6% in 2025, up from 98.2% in 2019.
facts.notes: Euro levels added run 12 from INSEE May-2026 vintage: EUR 3,306bn end-2024, EUR 3,460bn end-2025 [S042].

facts.statement: The French government deficit was 5.8% of GDP in 2024 and 5.2% in 2025; the deficit has not been below 2.3% at any point since 2018 despite record-high revenue.
French compulsory levies (taxes and social contributions) were 42.8% of GDP in 2024 and 43.6% in 2025, among the highest in the EU.
facts.notes: INSEE 'prelevements obligatoires' definition. Eurostat's tax-to-GDP ratio uses a different definition and yields a higher figure (~45-46%); do not mix the two series. EU ranking still needs a dedicated Eurostat check.

facts.statement: France spent 7.5 percentage points of GDP more than the euro area average in 2023 (57.0% vs 49.5%). Two-thirds of the gap is social protection (+5.0pp of GDP); the rest is economic affairs, housing and education. The gap has widened from 5.5pp in 2001.

France's GDP-per-capita gap with the US, reconciled on single datasets. World Bank WDI constant-2021-PPP series (change over time): France was 83.4% of the US level in 2000, 72.4% in 2024, 71.7% in 2025 - the gap widened from 16.6% to ~28% (about 11 points). Germany: 90.8% -> 82.8% (2024); Italy: 91.5% -> 70.4%. Banque de France (Eco Notepad 391, AMECO constant-2015-PPP): gaps 24%->33% France, 16->23 Germany, 18->36 Italy (2000->2023). The two vintages disagree on LEVELS (ICP benchmark revisions) but agree on the ~10-11-point widening and the ranking.
facts.notes: Q02 RESOLVED (run 12): the BdF-vs-WDI dispute is a PPP-vintage artifact (2011/2017/2021 ICP rounds moved France's measured 2000 position). RULES: never pair a BdF 2000 figure with a current-PPP level; the essay quotes the BdF series (one dataset, both years) with attribution, and the current-PPP level today (~27-28% below the US) as the level check. On current PPPs the gap has NOT widened since 2000 - the widening claim rests on constant-PPP series (both of them agree).

facts.statement: Decomposition of France's GDP-per-capita gap with the US: the largest part remains fewer hours worked per capita, but the hourly-productivity gap now accounts for more than one-third of the total (2023), versus a slightly negative contribution in 2000. France's productivity advantage has vanished and reversed.
facts.notes: Pivotal diagnostic fact: the gap is BOTH a labor-input problem and, increasingly, a productivity problem. Fixing only one does not close it.

facts.statement: Average annual hours worked per worker in France were below 1,500 in 2023, among the lowest in the OECD (with Germany, Denmark, Norway, Austria, Sweden, Netherlands, Iceland, Luxembourg, Finland). Countries like the US are near 1,800.
facts.notes: Hours per WORKER understate the French labor-input gap: employment rate and career length (late entry, early exit) matter as much. See F011/F012 backlog. Note Germany works even fewer hours per worker than France yet is richer per capita - the comparison cuts both ways and the essay must handle it honestly.

facts.statement: French R&D intensity has been flat for a decade: 2.22% of GDP in 2014, 2.18% in 2024 (provisional). Germany: 3.13% (2024). United States: 3.45% (2023). South Korea: 4.96% (2023). EU average: 2.26% (2023).
facts.notes: The gap is concentrated in BUSINESS R&D: EU business sector 1.49% of GDP vs US 2.70%, Korea 3.93% (2023). This despite France's Credit Impot Recherche being one of the most generous R&D tax credits in the OECD - a puzzle worth digging (backlog).

facts.statement: Draghi report: EU companies spent about half as much on R&I as a share of GDP as US companies (~EUR 270bn gap in 2021). The EU's top-3 corporate R&I spenders have remained automotive for two decades, while the US top-3 shifted from auto/pharma to software and digital. Draghi calls this the 'middle technology trap'.

Employment rate of the 55-64 (Eurostat, 2025): France 61.7%, Germany 75.3%, Sweden 78.3%, EU-27 66.4%. France gained 3.3 points in two years (2023: 58.4%) - the 2023 pension reform working through - but remains ~14 points below Germany. Per DARES, the entire remaining gap sits in the 60-64 bracket (10.7 points below the EU average in 2024); the French 55-59 employment rate is above the EU average.
facts.notes: Verified run 12 (Eurostat lfsi_emp_a). The 60-64 concentration sharpens the retirement-age lever: the gap is exactly where the effective exit age binds.

facts.statement: Hours worked per CAPITA (not per worker) in France are among the lowest in the OECD, roughly 600-650 hours/year vs ~800 in the US, because of lower employment rates at both ends of working life plus shorter hours.
facts.notes: Largely SUPERSEDED by F031 (verified): 673 hours/inhabitant (15-74) vs 776 Germany, 748 Sweden, 750 EU (Rexecode/OECD). Keep this entry only for the France-vs-US comparison, still to be computed from OECD data for the decomposition in F007.

facts.statement: France's potential growth is estimated at 0.9-1.2%/yr over 2026-2028 (Banque de France, OECD, IMF, European Commission all in that band), versus ~2%/yr before 2008. Banque de France estimates a durable -0.7% level scar on potential GDP vs the pre-Covid path.
facts.notes: Verified run 12 (BdF Eco Notepad 455, Jul 2026; AMECO; OECD EO; IMF WEO).

facts.statement: The French productivity puzzle, measured: market-sector productivity PER HEAD fell 8.5% below its 2010-2019 trend by mid-2023 (euro-area average: -2.4%); identified causes: apprenticeship boom 1.2pp, workforce composition 1.4pp, labor hoarding 1.7pp (temporary), lockdown scars 0.4pp - about 4.9pp explained. HOURLY productivity stood 4.9 points below trend in 2025 and only -0.8pt vs its 2019 level; Banque de France keeps a durable -2.7% loss in market-sector potential productivity.
facts.notes: Q01 LARGELY RESOLVED (run 12): about half the trend gap is composition (apprentices, hiring at the margin) and hoarding - i.e. partly the flip side of the employment gains; the durable structural loss is ~2.7%. Label the measure (per-head vs hourly) whenever quoted.

facts.statement: France's tax wedge on labor (single average worker, 2024) is 47.2% of labor cost - 3rd highest in the OECD after Belgium (52.6%) and Germany (47.9%), vs an OECD average of 34.9%. It has FALLEN from 50.4% in 2000. Net average tax rate on the worker: 28.1% vs OECD 25.0%.
facts.notes: CRITICAL NUANCE for C6: Germany's wedge is HIGHER than France's, yet Germany employs far more of its population. The naive 'taxes kill work' story fails against Germany; the French problem is the wedge COMBINED WITH retirement rules, late entry, and benefit design. The essay must use this honestly. Also: marginal wedges around the SMIC (contribution-relief phase-outs) can exceed 70-80% - a separate backlog fact worth adding.

facts.statement: French production taxes (levied on firms regardless of profit) were EUR 104bn in 2024 - 3.57% of GDP, three times the median of 13 European peers (1.2%) and roughly six times Germany's share (0.6%). On Eurostat's broader method: France 4.4% of GDP vs euro area 2.2% and Germany 1.0%. Germany collects almost four times less in absolute euros despite an economy 1.5x larger.
facts.notes: Two methodologies recorded on purpose (Montaigne includes CO2 tax and PEEC; Eurostat includes payroll-based taxes). Sweden is the only country higher (10.2% Eurostat) but its production taxes REPLACE social contributions - not comparable. Normalizing France to the peer median would return ~EUR 65-70bn/year to firms before profit.

facts.statement: Nuclear provided 67.1% of French mainland electricity generation in 2024 (361.7 of 539.0 TWh) and 68.1% in 2025 (373.0 of 547.5 TWh); nuclear + renewables reached a record 95.2% low-carbon generation in 2025, and France exported a record ~92 TWh.
facts.notes: Verified run 12 (RTE Bilan electrique 2025). Industrial electricity price comparison vs Germany still to add if the essay needs it [Q14].

facts.statement: France spends almost 14% of GDP on public pensions (EUR 388.4bn) - four points of GDP more than Germany (Cour des comptes, Feb 2025). French retirees' standard of living roughly equals that of working people, with a LOWER poverty rate; in Germany and the OECD average, retirees live slightly below workers.
facts.notes: Primary institutional source (Cour des comptes). Consistent with F005 (social protection = 2/3 of spending gap) and S008 (pensions drove the 2024 spending increase). The 'retirees live as well as workers' point is the sharpest single illustration of the intergenerational trade. UPDATE run 12: COR annual report (Jun 2025) puts 2024 pensions at EUR 407bn / 13.9% of GDP - use the 2024 figure with F051's same-year education comparison; the 4-points-vs-Germany structural gap is unchanged.

facts.statement: France ranked #1 in Europe for foreign direct investment projects for the 7th consecutive year (EY European Attractiveness Survey 2026): 852 projects in 2025 vs UK 730, Germany 548. Caveat quantified: France attracts ~33-35 jobs per project vs 49 (Germany) and 61 (UK); it ranked only 3rd in FDI job creation in 2024.
facts.notes: Verified run 12. Use with the jobs-per-project caveat: the ranking measures project count, not scale.

facts.statement: French unemployment fell from ~10.4% (2015 annual average) to 7.4% (2024 annual average) - a three-point fall over the reform decade (2017 ordinances, apprenticeship expansion, unemployment-insurance reform), to lows unseen since the early 1980s. THE TREND THEN REVERSED: 7.7% average in 2025, 8.3% in Q2 2026 (highest since Q3 2020), as growth stalled and parts of the reforms were suspended or unwound.
facts.notes: Verified run 12 (INSEE IR 192, Aug 2026). Two-sided by design: the fall proves reforms move the needle; the 2025-26 rise must appear wherever the fall is quoted - it also ILLUSTRATES the ratchet (C4): reforms un-passed, results un-earned. Do not attribute the rise solely to reversal (the cycle turned too).

facts.statement: The French public's hostility to capitalism is real, recent and stable: 62% of French respondents held a negative opinion of capitalism in Dec 2021 (64% in 2019, Odoxa). In a 34-country peer-reviewed survey (Zitelmann 2023), France sits firmly in the anti-capitalist group; 'capitalism leads to growing inequality' ranks as the #1 criticism in France. Pro-capitalist attitudes dominate in only 6-7 of 34 countries surveyed (led by Poland, the US, Czechia, Japan, South Korea - and Sweden when the word 'capitalism' is avoided).
facts.notes: Upgraded from the stale 2005 GlobeScan datum. Caveats kept honest: Zitelmann is an identified pro-market advocate (published peer-reviewed; methodology described); Odoxa is a single-country commercial barometer. Interesting detail for the essay: Sweden reads pro-market when 'capitalism' is described rather than named - the WORD carries weight. Also from Odoxa: French executives (58%) and the affluent (47% negative) accept capitalism far more than workers (69% negative) - the divide is distributional, not uniform.

facts.statement: France's PISA 2022 mathematics score fell 21 points vs 2018 (495 -> 474), the sharpest drop in the French series - but the OECD average fell ~15 points in the same COVID-marked cycle and at least seven OECD countries fell more (Iceland -36, Norway -33, Poland -27, Netherlands -26, Germany -25). France now sits AT the OECD average (474 vs 472). Over 2012-2022 the share of French students below proficiency Level 2 rose from 22.4% to 29%.
facts.notes: Verified run 12. CORRECTION recorded: 'one of the largest declines among rich countries' was wrong - the correct sharp formulation is 'unprecedented for France; France is now exactly average'. ALSO REFUTED (OECD + DEPP concur): the decline was NOT concentrated among weaker students - high and low achievers fell similarly 2018-2022, and over 2012-2022 the 90th percentile fell more. The essay must not claim bottom-concentration; the below-Level-2 share rise is the defensible bottom-end fact.

facts.statement: French households save 17.9% of disposable income (2025, a near-record; financial saving 10.5% of income - above German households for the first time since 2000) and hold EUR 6,590bn of financial wealth (end-2025): roughly twice the public debt and 2.7 times the CAC 40's market capitalization. But only EUR 310bn sits in directly-held listed shares; interest-rate products total EUR 3,911bn vs EUR 2,576bn in equity-type products. Regulated savings accounts hold EUR 947bn; euro-fund life insurance EUR 1,571bn. Insurers alone hold ~10% of the State's debt.
facts.notes: The core capital-misallocation fact: the world's most anti-capitalist rich public (F021) holds a savings pool the size of two national debts, allocated to lending its own state money. 58% of placements stay in France, 80% in the euro area - the home bias means redirection is plumbing, not patriotism. Rexecode's line fits: 'the French save a lot, but have little savings' (low-yield allocation).

facts.statement: French state debt-interest charge is projected at EUR 64.8bn in 2026 and EUR 74.2bn in 2027 (+EUR 12.3bn of constrained spending in the 2027 ceilings, alongside +EUR 6.4bn for defense) - interest is the fastest-growing budget item.
facts.notes: State scope only. General-government scope is larger (~EUR 78bn in 2026, ~2.6% of GDP per HCFP). Do not mix scopes in one series - see F025 note.

facts.statement: Unchanged-policy trajectory (Jaravel/Ragot/Tavernier/Valla report to the Finance Ministry, July 2026): deficit widens to 5.9% of GDP in 2027 and ~6.8-7% by 2030; debt peaks at 130.5% of GDP; general-government interest reaches ~EUR 124bn by 2030 (+EUR 46bn vs 2026), growing ~5x faster than the economy. Stabilizing debt requires ~EUR 126bn of cumulative adjustment by 2032 (~EUR 25bn/year).
facts.notes: Verified against two independent press accounts of the report; a future run should fetch the primary 37-page report and re-check the figures. The 2021-2030 interest comparison (EUR 40bn to 124bn) mixes state and general-government scopes - use with care.

facts.statement: France lost its double-A rating in autumn 2025: Fitch cut AA- to A+ (12 Sep 2025, lowest French rating on record), S&P cut AA- to A+ in an unscheduled move (17 Oct 2025), Moody's kept Aa3 but went negative outlook (24 Oct 2025). The 10-year OAT-Bund spread settled around 80-83bp by March 2026, versus a 20-40bp historical norm; the 10-year OAT yield traded near Italy's.
facts.notes: Ratings: high confidence (multiple primary press). Spread level: medium - re-verify against market data or Banque de France; note S&P cited the suspension of the 2023 pension reform as a driver. Also note the EDHEC point: markets barely reacted to the downgrades themselves - the risk was already priced.

facts.statement: France's debt grows much faster than its economy (INSEE, May 2026 vintage). 2025: general-government deficit EUR 152.5bn (5.1% of GDP) against nominal GDP growth of EUR 55.8bn - 2.7 euros borrowed per euro of new economy. 2024: EUR 169.1bn against EUR 101.4bn (1.7 per euro). 2023 was inflation-flattered: EUR 151.9bn against EUR 179.8bn. Maastricht debt: EUR 3,103bn (end-2023), 3,306bn (end-2024, +203), 3,460bn (end-2025, +154). Nominal GDP 2025: EUR 2,991bn.
facts.notes: Q09 RESOLVED (run 12): euro-level series built from INSEE IR 78 + IP 2105/2106. HONESTY RULES: (1) this is an accounting contrast, not a causal multiplier - the essay says 'added X of debt for every euro of new economy', never 'debt bought growth'; (2) the ratio swings with inflation (2023 was below 1 because nominal GDP surged) - the multi-year trend is carried by the debt/GDP ratio itself (109.5% -> 112.6% -> 115.7%), and the inflation objection is answered separately [F074]; (3) 2025 nominal growth (+1.9%) was disinflation-dampened - quote 2024 alongside 2025, never 2025 alone.

facts.statement: Non-residents held 54.6% of French general-government long-term debt securities at end-2025, up from 52.8% at end-2024. Outstanding general-government debt securities: ~EUR 3,039bn (of which EUR 2,717bn for the State).
facts.notes: Settles the Japan counterargument to C7: Japan's debt is held domestically and issued in a currency Japan prints; over half of French debt is held abroad in a currency France does not control. Holders: euro-area, UK, US institutions (pension funds, central banks, insurers).

facts.statement: France's gross medium/long-term debt issuance (net of buybacks) was EUR 300bn in 2025 and is programmed at EUR 310bn for 2026 - roughly EUR 6bn to raise every week. Amortizations alone rise to EUR 175.8bn in 2026. Counterpoint kept honest: the weighted average rate on MLT issuance FELL to 2.78% in 2025 from 3.06% in 2024 as the ECB eased.
facts.notes: Two-sided fact by design. The refinancing wall is real (interest compounds as old low-coupon debt rolls into 2.5-3.5% paper), but 2025 issuance conditions EASED - the essay must not imply an ongoing rate spiral. The squeeze is stock-driven (volume), not only rate-driven.

facts.statement: Aligning France's employment rate on Germany's (gap: 8.7 points in 2022, 68.1% vs 76.8%) would create +1.5 million jobs and raise GDP by +3.2% after adjusting for Germany's higher part-time share - or +3.6 million jobs and +7.0% GDP unadjusted. Fiscal effect of the adjusted scenario: ~EUR 38bn of additional general-government revenue, ~EUR 20bn improvement of the social-protection balance (DG Tresor for the HCFiPS).
facts.notes: Government primary source (DG Tresor note for the Haut Conseil du financement de la protection sociale). The gap concentrates on the young and seniors. This is the single most bankable number of the solution thesis: the labor lever is worth 3-7% of GDP in LEVEL, plus a large fiscal double dividend.

facts.statement: France works 673 hours per year per inhabitant (15-74), vs 750 EU average, 776 Germany, 748 Sweden - a deficit of 6% vs the EU and 9% vs Germany/Sweden. Employment deficit vs Germany: 2.8 million jobs; vs Nordics: 4 million. Aligning labor quantity on Germany/Sweden would add up to +5% of GDP net of the lower productivity of added workers (+3% on the EU average). Rexecode's conclusion: the single most effective lever is raising the effective retirement age.
facts.notes: Employer-side think tank (leaning noted) but the hours data is OECD/Eurostat-based and consistent with S020's government numbers. Supersedes the rough estimate previously in F012 (which compared to the US; the relevant policy benchmark is Germany/Nordics). France's demographic structure (smaller working-age share) explains part of the per-inhabitant gap - the fixable part is employment rates at BOTH ends of working life.

facts.statement: EDF's programme of six EPR2 reactors (Penly, Gravelines, Bugey) is costed at EUR 72.8bn in 2020 euros (~EUR 83bn in 2025 euros), presented as a ceiling - up ~40% from the initial 2022 estimate of EUR 51.7bn. First reactor targeted for 2038, then one every 12-18 months. Final investment decision expected end-2026, with state support: a subsidised loan covering at least 50% of construction and a 40-year contract-for-difference.
facts.notes: Company primary source. Two-sided by design: the asset (F017) is real but the delivery risk is real too - +40% cost drift BEFORE construction start, and Flamanville's history behind it. The solution thesis must treat new nuclear as a bet with a risk budget, not a free lunch.

facts.statement: At the Paris AI Action Summit (February 2025), EUR 109bn of private AI infrastructure commitments for France were announced; by spring 2026, over EUR 50bn of AI datacenter projects were underway, making France the largest AI datacenter build-out in Europe (Nvidia, Microsoft, Brookfield, MGX among investors), explicitly anchored on nuclear power availability.
facts.notes: The 109bn announcement is widely documented; the follow-through figure (50bn underway) comes from a niche tech outlet - re-source from primary (Elysee, France 2030) before the essay leans on the second number. Evidence that the nuclear-AI thesis (C10) is not hypothetical: the market is already voting.

facts.statement: Canonical growth-education elasticity (OECD 2010, 'The High Cost of Low Educational Performance', Hanushek & Woessmann): 1.74pp of annual per-capita growth per standard deviation (100 PISA points); a +25-point improvement yields ~+0.47pp of annual long-run growth once the improved cohorts fill the labor force. Contested: Komatsu & Rappleye (2017) show the correlation weakens when scores are matched to subsequent growth; endogeneity concerns make it an upper bound.
facts.notes: Verified run 12 with the critique recorded. The model already halves the elasticity (model.py) - keep that haircut; treat as upper bound, not forecast.

facts.statement: Causal evidence that market participation changes values: in a field experiment (2,700 adults, England), randomly assigned stock investment (GBP 50, 6 weeks) shifted socio-economic values rightward by 9-12% of the Labour-Conservative gap - on merit, personal responsibility, redistribution - with effects persisting a year later, driven by familiarity with and reduced distrust of markets.
facts.notes: Margalit & Shayo, AJPS 2021. The core causal anchor for C12. Honest limits: individual-level, GBP 50 stakes, 6-week exposure; national-scale, own-money, decade-long effects are an extrapolation - but the DIRECTION and MECHANISM (familiarity, distrust reduction) are exactly what C12 claims.

facts.statement: Second causal anchor: squatters in Buenos Aires who received land titles through an exogenous allocation developed markedly more pro-market beliefs (individualism, materialism, merit) - a 'market beliefs' index 20% higher than untitled neighbors living otherwise identical lives, converging to the general population's beliefs.
facts.notes: Di Tella, Galiani & Schargrodsky, QJE 2007. Property ownership, not just financial assets - complements F035: two different asset classes, two methods, same direction. Beliefs follow ownership.

facts.statement: Long-run elasticity of multifactor productivity to R&D (OECD panel, 16 countries, 1980-98): +1% business R&D -> +0.13% MFP; +1% public R&D -> +0.17%; +1% foreign R&D -> ~+0.45%. Effects are larger in countries more intensive in business R&D.
facts.notes: The model's TFP calibration [model.py, A6]. Caveats: 2001 study, averages across countries/time; France's low business-R&D intensity means the marginal effect could be below average initially. The foreign-R&D elasticity is a reminder that ABSORPTION (diffusion) matters as much as domestic spending - supports adding a diffusion component to Lever 3.

facts.statement: France's demographic advantage is expiring: fertility fell to 1.56 (2025) and INSEE's central 2026 projection assumes 1.45 from 2028. Population peaks at 69.8M in 2037 then declines to 65.9M by 2070 (central); the ACTIVE population peaks around 2040 then falls; the 20-64 share drops from 55.3% (2026) to 54.0% (2050) and 51.7% (2070); the old-age dependency ratio rises from 40 (2026) to 62 (2070). Central migration assumption: +150k/year.
facts.notes: CORRECTS C5: 'France has better demographics than Germany/Italy' is true of today's STOCK, not tomorrow's FLOW - the fertility collapse (2.0 in 2010 -> 1.45 assumed) erodes the advantage from the 2040s. Consequences: (a) the labor lever's ceiling shrinks after 2045; (b) family policy and skilled immigration become GROWTH policy, currently absent from the program [Q16]; (c) aging adds a slow fiscal shock on top of the debt (C7).

facts.statement: A single cluster of French size-contingent regulations (labor laws binding at 50 employees) acts as a 2.3% implicit tax on labor and costs ~3.4% of GDP in welfare under observed French wage rigidity (1.3% if wages were fully flexible). Main losers: workers; main winners: small firms staying small.
facts.notes: Garicano-Lelarge-Van Reenen, AER 2016 (data 1995-2007; thresholds partially softened since - check post-2019 PACTE reforms before quoting as current). Anchors the reallocation lever (L2 in model.py): if ONE distortion cluster costs 3.4%, a broad simplification agenda claiming +2.5% of GDP level is conservative in spirit, though the essay must not sum distortion studies naively.

facts.statement: Sweden's post-1991 turnaround, verified: public expenditure peaked at ~70% of GDP (1993, deficit 11.2%), fell to 58% by 1998 and ~51% by 2007. The Lindbeck Commission (appointed Dec 1992, reported March 1993) delivered 113 proposals that were implemented CONSISTENTLY ACROSS ALTERNATING governments (social-democrat and centre-right): multi-year expenditure ceilings, local balanced-budget rules, independent central bank, the 1999 NDC pension reform with automatic demographic balancing, broad privatizations. Composition of the cuts 1993-2000 (total -9.5pp of GDP): social protection -3.3, housing subsidies -1.9, economic affairs -1.9 - while HEALTH (-0.1) and EDUCATION (-0.2) were left nearly untouched.
facts.notes: Validates comparable X01 and supplies the thesis's two key Swedish lessons: (1) composition - cut transfers and subsidies, protect schools and hospitals; (2) process - the plan was PRE-WRITTEN by an expert commission in 3 months and survived changes of government. Honest caveat kept: even Sweden's 'automatic' pension brake was softened politically when it bit (2009-10) - no design fully escapes politics.

facts.statement: EC 2024 Ageing Report baselines: EU potential GDP growth averages 1.3%/yr over 2022-2070 (1.1% in the lower-TFP sensitivity, which the report itself flags as a considerable risk since the baseline assumes a reversal of the decades-long TFP decline). Germany's potential growth declines from ~1.4 toward ~1.0 across the horizon (country fiche). TWO-SIDED for France: the report projects French total age-related expenditure FALLING over 2022-2070 under current legislation - because current indexation rules mechanically erode relative pension generosity.
facts.notes: Calibrates the model's comparison baseline (A3) - now run with a Germany sensitivity row. The French finding must be handled honestly by C11: on paper, current-law pension spending declines long-run; the catch is that the decline works through politically fragile indexation erosion (the same politics that suspended the 2023 reform), and the report's own low-TFP scenario shows the baseline is optimistic. Exact per-capita paths by country still to extract from the statistical annex [Q18].

facts.statement: Housing (incl. water/energy) is French households' largest expense: 27.8% of final consumption in 2024 (food 15.6%, transport 12.7%; includes owner-occupiers' imputed rents). Real house prices doubled from 2000 to the 2022 peak (OECD real index 58 -> 120, 2015=100) and stand ~+77% vs 2000 after the correction. Housing starts fell to 274,611 in 2025 vs the 2006 record of 494,000.
facts.notes: Verified run 12 (INSEE portrait social 2025; OECD analytical house prices; SDES Sitadel).

facts.statement: France's immigration is weakly employment-oriented, verified (2024): of 343,024 first residence permits, 58,374 (17.0%) were economic; students 32.3%, family 26.4%, humanitarian 15.9% (Ministere de l'Interieur/DGEF). Canada: the economic class was 58.2% of 483,640 permanent admissions in 2024 (IRCC).
facts.notes: Verified run 12. Definitional caveat when quoting: France counts first permits incl. temporary (students) and excludes EU citizens; Canada counts permanent admissions and its economic class includes dependents. The 17-vs-58 contrast survives the caveat.

facts.statement: Fertility and family policy, verified: French TFR was 2.02 in 2010 (2nd in the EU behind Ireland, 1st for most of the 2010s), 1.61 in 2024, 1.56 in 2025 - the lowest since the end of WWI; deaths exceeded births in 2025 for the first time since 1945 (INSEE Bilan demographique 2025). Policy timeline confirmed: quotient familial cap cut 2013 (EUR 2,336 -> 2,000) and 2014 (-> 1,500); allocations familiales means-modulated from July 2015 (~EUR 760mn/yr saved). France's family-policy effort (~3.6% of GDP, IGAS broad measure) was the OECD's highest on that measure. The fertility slide began in 2015; chronology verified, causality contested.
facts.notes: Verified run 12. CORRECTIONS: 2010 rank was 2nd (behind Ireland), not 1st; 'highest in OECD' holds only on the broad IGAS measure (OECD's own PF1.1 names Iceland/Poland). The fertility-intentions gap (~2.3 desired) still to pin separately [Q21]. Frame causality as hypothesis; chronology (2013-15 cuts, 2015-on slide) as fact.

facts.statement: France is the #4 origin country of elite (top-2%) AI researchers worldwide - after the US, China and India, with ~4% of the global pool (MacroPolo Global AI Talent Tracker 2.0, 2023, NeurIPS-based; origin = undergraduate degree) - and the largest European source. A large share of European top-tier AI talent outside academia works for American companies; MacroPolo notes France 'notably improved retention' recently.
facts.notes: Verified run 12. CORRECTED: 'most work in US labs' is not published for France specifically - say 'a large share work for US labs'. Tracker frozen at 2023; do not cite unofficial 3.0 versions. Broader expatriation data (CAE, Ordre des medecins) still unverified.

facts.statement: The anti-system vote roughly rose from a third to half of first-round votes in twenty years. 2002 presidential R1: Le Pen + Megret + far left + PCF ~33%. 2022 presidential R1 (Conseil constitutionnel): Le Pen 23.15 + Zemmour 7.07 + Melenchon 21.95 = 52.2% (57.8% adding smaller anti-system candidates). 2024 European: RN 31.4 + Reconquete 5.5 + LFI 9.9 = 46.7%.
facts.notes: Verified run 12. Definition must be named when quoted (which candidates counted); 'roughly half' holds on the narrow three-candidate definition in 2022, slightly below half in 2024.

facts.statement: French school equity, verified: socio-economic status explains 21% of the variance in PISA 2022 math performance in France vs 15% OECD average; the advantaged-disadvantaged gap is 113 points vs 93 OECD - among the strongest social determinism in the OECD. Teacher pay: starting salaries reached the OECD average after the 2023 attractiveness measures, but at 15 years' experience France pays ~USD 53k (PPP) vs an OECD ~62k and roughly HALF of Germany's level.
facts.notes: Verified run 12. TWO CORRECTIONS: (1) 'starting salaries below OECD average' is outdated (2023 measures closed it); the mid-career gap vs Germany (~2x) is the live fact. (2) The 'math decline concentrated among weaker students' leg is REFUTED (see F022) - the equity claim rests on the SES gradient, not on the decline's distribution. 'Among the most class-determined' is the defensible superlative, not 'the most'.

facts.statement: French universities are funded at roughly EUR 11-12k per student per year - a fraction of US research universities and below northern-European levels; France places only a handful of universities in global top-100 rankings despite its elite-math tradition (most Fields medals per capita among large countries).
facts.notes: BACKLOG: OECD Education at a Glance, ARWU/THE rankings, Fields medal counts. The paradox to exploit: world-class inputs (prepas, ENS math), underfunded and rigidly governed universities.

facts.statement: France has 11.3 professional judges per 100,000 inhabitants (7,690 judges) vs a Council of Europe median of 17.7 and an EU-27 median of 22.9 (CEPEJ 2024 evaluation, 2022 data). Prisons: occupancy 141.3% overall and 174.5% in maisons d'arret (July 2026, record 89,446 detainees for 63,289 places).
facts.notes: Verified run 12. The old '>120%' understated: ~140% overall, ~175% in remand prisons. When quoting the judges median, name which one (CoE 17.7 or EU-27 22.9).

facts.statement: The wealth-tax alternative, with verified numbers: the ISF yielded ~EUR 5.0-5.2bn/yr in its final years (2015-2017, DGFiP). Zucman's proposed 2% minimum tax on fortunes above EUR 100mn (~1,800 households): ~EUR 20bn/yr central estimate by its author (15-25 range); economists applying the CAE's behavioral elasticities (Bach, Bozio et al., Focus 118, Jul 2025) put the yield near EUR 5bn. The bill passed the Assemblee in Feb 2025 and was rejected by the Senate in Jun 2025. Even the optimistic estimate covers roughly a fifth of the program's annual financing needs and none of the labor-supply gap.
facts.notes: Verified run 12. The yield is disputed by a factor of four between camps - quote both numbers; the essay's argument (complement, not alternative) survives on either.

facts.statement: France spends about twice as much on public pensions as on its entire education system - and 2.6x on a public-vs-public basis. Same-year comparison (2024): pensions EUR 407bn / 13.9% of GDP (COR, June 2025) vs total education spending (DIE, public+private) EUR 197.1bn / 6.8% of GDP (DEPP) = 2.04x. Eurostat COFOG public-only (2024): old-age 13.4% of GDP vs education 5.1% = 2.63x (EU-27: 10.7 vs 4.8).
facts.notes: Verified run 12 on same-year 2024 data. 'Roughly twice' is the conservative floor (DIE includes private spending); public-vs-public the ratio is ~2.6. F018's EUR 388bn was the 2023 vintage - use EUR 407bn (2024, COR) going forward.

facts.statement: Flamanville 3 (EPR): budgeted EUR 3.3bn with service planned for June 2012 (2004); construction cost EUR 12.4bn-2015 (Cour des comptes 2020; EDF's 2022 revision: 13.2), full cost ~EUR 19.1bn-2015 including financing (Cour 2020), raised to EUR 20.4bn-2015 / 23.7bn-2023 at completion (Cour, Jan 2025). Grid connection 21 December 2024 - about 12.5 years late. EDF net financial debt: EUR 51.5bn (end-2025).
facts.notes: Verified run 12 (Cour des comptes 2020 + Jan 2025 follow-up; EDF FY2025 results). 'Four times over budget' matches construction cost (3.8-4x); the full-cost multiple is ~6x - the essay's phrasing ('four times over budget and twelve years late') is the conservative version.

facts.statement: French hourly productivity LEVEL is world-class: GDP per hour worked (OECD, current PPPs, 2024): France USD 92.7, Germany 100.7, United States 100.1, UK 85.7, Italy 80.7, OECD 78.7. France/US = 92.6% (a ~7% gap), France/Germany = 92.1%. The French problem is the QUANTITY of labor (hours per capita) and the GROWTH of productivity, not workers' hourly performance.
facts.notes: Verified run 12. Current-PPP levels move with ICP benchmark revisions (the 2021 round lifted Europe vs the US): 'within ~10% of the US' is the safe phrasing; on BdF constant-2015-PPP accounting the hourly gap is larger [F006 notes]. Norway, Denmark, Belgium, Luxembourg (and artificially Ireland) rank above France.

facts.statement: US life expectancy gaps by income are extreme (Chetty et al. 2016, JAMA, 2001-2014 tax records): 14.6 years between top-1% and bottom-1% incomes for men, 10.1 for women (at age 40). Over 2001-2014, the top 5% gained ~2.3-2.9 years of life expectancy; the bottom 5% gained ~0.3 (men) / 0.04 (women) - stagnation at the bottom despite frontier GDP growth.
facts.notes: Verified run 12. Attribute precisely: the stagnation finding is for the bottom 5% (not quartile); the 14.6/10.1 gaps are top-1% vs bottom-1% at age 40.

facts.statement: The US spends 17.2% of GDP on health vs France 11.5% (2024, OECD Health at a Glance 2025) - USD 14,885 vs 7,367 per capita PPP - for life expectancy of 78.4 years vs France's 83.0 (2023). Germany (12.3%) now outspends France in Europe.
facts.notes: Verified run 12. The gap is 5.7 points of GDP - 'nearly six points', not five.

facts.statement: The Germany check likely cuts against the naive version of the argument: France's poverty rate after transfers (~14%) is LOWER than Germany's at-risk-of-poverty rate (~16-21% depending on measure); German bottom-decile real wages stagnated or fell from the mid-1990s to ~2015 (Hartz-era wage restraint, mini-jobs), with partial catch-up only after the 2015 minimum wage. Germany's growth did NOT straightforwardly lift its bottom quartile faster than redistributive France.
facts.notes: REFUTED as stated, run 15 (Q25 load-bearing half resolved): on Eurostat SILC 2024 the poverty rates are a statistical tie (FR 15.9 vs DE 15.5) and Germany's P10 is 8% ABOVE France's - see F097 for the full resolution (France led until ~2016; Germany caught up; housing nets the floors back to parity; the OECD's SOEP-based reading still favors France - survey-dependent). The German-bottom-stagnation half of this fact was CONFIRMED and lives as F098. Kept per protocol so no future run re-adds the dead version.

facts.statement: UK rail privatization, verified: average annual government support tripled in real terms - GBP 1.7bn/yr (five years to 1991/92) vs GBP 5.3bn/yr (five years to 2017/18), both in 2017/18 prices (ORR data); GBP 11.9bn in 2024/25. Railtrack collapsed into Network Rail (Oct 2002). Renationalization: operators from 2018 (LNER), Public Ownership Act Nov 2024, all DfT operators public by end-2027; Great British Railways bill Nov 2025.
facts.notes: Verified run 12. Subsidy comparisons sensitive to scope (HS2/Crossrail, Network Rail loans excluded from the tripling figure); direction holds on every basis.

facts.statement: The health-efficiency frontier, verified (OECD Health at a Glance 2025: spending 2024 % GDP / life expectancy 2023): France 11.5 / 83.0; Spain 9.2 / 84.0; Italy 8.4 / 83.5; Korea 8.4 / 83.5; Israel 7.6 / 83.8; Singapore (WHO) 4.5 / 83.7. Several universal systems deliver French-level or better longevity for 2-7 points of GDP less.
facts.notes: Verified run 12. Life expectancy is a crude outcome proxy but treatable-mortality data points the same way; Singapore's compulsory-savings model limits comparability - lead with Spain (universal, European, 2.3 points cheaper, longer lives).

facts.statement: Evidence on small user frictions in healthcare: the RAND Health Insurance Experiment found modest cost-sharing reduced utilization with no adverse effect on AVERAGE health - but it cut appropriate and inappropriate care alike, with harm concentrated on the poorest and sickest; separately, behavioral studies (e.g. Waber et al. 2008) find priced treatments are perceived as more effective than free ones. Small copays (the author's 1-2 euro intuition) have real behavioral effects and real distributional risks - design matters (caps, exemptions).
facts.notes: BACKLOG: RAND HIE canonical papers (Newhouse et al.), Waber et al. JAMA 2008; also France's own franchises medicales (2008-) as domestic evidence. Supports smart-friction design within a free-at-point-of-need system, with the distributional caveat stated.

facts.statement: The How Asia Works thesis (Studwell 2013): Japan, Korea, Taiwan (and later China) developed through a dirigiste sequence - radical land reform, then EXPORT-DISCIPLINED industrial policy (state support strictly conditional on success in world markets, with systematic culling of losers), then financial repression steering household savings into industry. The mechanism is not state betting per se but the DISCIPLINE: subsidies died when firms failed abroad. Import-substitution dirigisme without export discipline (Latin America, Southeast Asia) failed with the same tools.
facts.notes: Verified as an accurate account of the book's argument (widely reviewed). Relevance to the program: France's dirigiste FORM is legitimate for long-horizon capital (energy, compute, rail) where private horizons are too short - but France's failure mode is refusing to cull (supporting incumbents forever). Hence the program rule: every state bet carries a kill criterion (C21). France's own record fits Studwell's split: nuclear/TGV/Airbus had verifiable engineering targets and export markets; Plan Calcul, Minitel, Bull had neither.

facts.statement: Dismissal for professional insufficiency in the French State civil service: 13 cases in 2022, across ~2.5 million agents (DGAFP figures released in the April 2024 reform debate; plus 222 disciplinary revocations). No official aggregate exists for all three branches of the fonction publique (5.80 million agents at end-2023, DGAFP/INSEE).
facts.notes: Verified run 12 - best available figure, State service only, ministry data cited in the reform debate rather than a published series (hence confidence medium). CORRECTED: the old 'a hundred cases across 5.7mn' both overstated the count and mixed scopes; the true rarity is starker.

facts.statement: GDP understates modern quality-of-life gains: free digital goods carry large consumer surplus invisible in national accounts (Brynjolfsson et al.'s GDP-B experiments value free services like search, maps, messaging at hundreds of euros per user-year). Technology diffusion - historically driven by growth - raises the quality of life of ALL quartiles through channels income statistics miss.
facts.notes: BACKLOG: Brynjolfsson, Collis et al. GDP-B papers (AER Insights 2019+). Supports the author's second success criterion: the 75%'s quality of life includes technology-driven surplus, which is a GROWTH product - an argument for growth that does not run through redistribution at all.

facts.statement: Innovators capture ~2.2% of the social surplus their innovations create (range 1.3-3.3% across specifications); ~98% flows to consumers (Nordhaus 2004, NBER WP 10433, US nonfarm business 1948-2001, from ~7% instantaneous appropriability and ~20%/yr profit depreciation).
facts.notes: Verified run 12. Cite as an order of magnitude: an economy-wide average under strong assumptions; excludes rents captured via founder equity or star wages; says nothing about marginal innovations.

facts.statement: French grid carbon intensity (Ember, 2026 release): 40.5 gCO2e/kWh (2024), 41.4 (2025) - vs Germany 336/330 and EU average 211/210. France is about one-eighth of Germany's intensity and one-fifth of the EU's; RTE's direct-emissions method gives France ~20g.
facts.notes: Verified run 12. CORRECTED: Germany is ~330 (not 350-400) and the EU ~210 (not 230-250) - both fell. Use one methodology (Ember lifecycle-type) consistently across geographies; 'a tenth of Germany's' overstated - 'an eighth' is right.

facts.statement: Absolute decoupling is observed, France included: over 2005-2023 French GDP grew +21.8% while consumption-based CO2 fell -25.3% (545 -> 407 Mt; Global Carbon Project / World Bank via OWID). Peer-reviewed anchor: Le Quere et al. 2019 (Nature Climate Change) documents 18 developed economies cutting CO2 on both territorial and consumption bases while growing (2005-2015); broader recent counts find 30+ (up to ~39) countries absolutely decoupled per capita on a consumption basis.
facts.notes: Verified run 12. Lead with the France-specific numbers (grew a fifth, cut a quarter, imports included); use '18 in peer-reviewed work, 30+ on broader counts' rather than a naked '30+'. CEPII caveat: France's consumption-based decline concentrates after ~2008.

facts.statement: Administered vs market pricing, with numbers: French medecins liberaux averaged EUR 124,000/yr of activity income in 2021 (GPs EUR 98,300; other specialists EUR 153,300 - DREES), with 92% of income at CNAM-set tariffs. The top 1% of private-sector salaried posts starts at ~EUR 122,600/yr net (INSEE 2023); salaried heads of 500+ employee firms average ~EUR 203,000/yr net; finance-market cadres ~EUR 132,000. An average GP earns ~3.5x the average private wage yet sits below the top-1% threshold and at roughly half a big-firm executive's pay.
facts.notes: Verified run 12. The 'administered tariffs' clause is an interpretation (DREES documents the tariff structure, makes no causal claim); sector-2 extra billing is the escape valve. The clean version remains the PRICING MECHANISM contrast.

facts.statement: The 'second line' verified (DARES-CEET 2021): 17 occupations, 4.6 million private-sector employees kept France running through lockdowns - drivers, cleaners, cashiers, home-care aides, security guards, construction and agri-food workers. Their average full-time wage was ~30% below the private-sector average (EUR 1,634 vs 2,337 net/month), and the gap widens with age (-37% at 55-59).
facts.notes: Verified run 12. Private sector only; excludes the medical 'first line'.

facts.statement: The historical high-water mark, verified: French GDP per capita was 54.2% of the US level in 1950 (Maddison 2023, 2011 int'l $) and converged to ~79.5% by 1975-1980 (series peak 82.6% in 1982, flattered by the US recession) - the closest any large European country came. At market exchange rates, France MATCHED the US in 1980: $12,565 vs $12,575 (World Bank current-US$, 99.9%). French output per HOUR surpassed the US level around 2000 [F007].
facts.notes: Verified run 12. CORRECTED: 'matched', never 'exceeded' (current WDI vintage puts France $10 below); 85% PPP never reached. The 1980 parity is a currency phenomenon (strong franc, pre-Volcker dollar) - the essay's 'in the dollars of the day' phrasing is exactly right.

facts.statement: The French electorate skews old, and turnout skews it further (INSEE, 2022 elections): systematic abstention is 24% among under-35 registered voters vs ~9% for the 50-69; at the presidential first round, 67% of 18-29s voted vs 77% of 65+; at the legislative second round, 28% of under-30s voted vs 59% of 65+. COMPUTED (registered voters by age x INSEE turnout by age, cross-checked against Ipsos day-of surveys): voters aged 55+ cast a MAJORITY of all ballots at the 2022 legislative elections (~53% INSEE-based, ~56% Ipsos-based, both rounds), about half at the higher-turnout 2024 legislatives (~50-51%), and 45-48% at the 2022 presidential. Baseline: 55+ were 43.6% of registered voters in 2022, 44.2% in 2024 - the share rises mechanically every year.
facts.notes: Q32 RESOLVED (run 12). Method: INSEE registered rolls by age bracket x INSEE participation-survey turnout by age (signature lists, not self-reports); both methods reproduce official aggregate turnout within ~1pp. Caveats recorded: the 55+ split of INSEE's 30-64 bracket uses proportional rescaling of the detailed profile; Ipsos's single 70+ bracket overstates old-age turnout slightly; truth likely between the two columns. ROBUST FORMULATION for the essay: majority at the 2022 legislatives, about half at the higher-turnout 2024 ones, approaching half at presidentials. The 2024 nuance is stated, not hidden: when turnout surges the majority thins to half - the impasse softens at the edges but the median voter of pension law remains 55+.

facts.statement: Germany's constitution gives the not-yet-born justiciable standing; France's does not on fiscal matters. The Bundesverfassungsgericht (24 March 2021) held Art. 20a of the Basic Law to be 'a justiciable legal provision', ruled that fundamental rights operate as 'intertemporal guarantees of freedom' protecting against burdens 'unilaterally offloaded onto the future', recognized an objective duty to protect future generations who 'do not yet carry any fundamental rights', and struck down parts of the federal climate law on that basis. Germany's constitutional debt brake (Art. 109/115 GG) applies the same intergenerational logic to borrowing itself. France's closest equivalent - the 2004 environmental charter, as read by the Conseil constitutionnel in 2023 - covers only environmental harms, with no fiscal counterpart.
facts.notes: The BVerfG holdings are verified against the court's official English text. Two flags: the debt-brake intergenerational framing and the exact scope of the French 2023 CC decision still need their own citations [Q33]. For C25: this is the institutional half of the impasse - the German political system is constitutionally FORCED to represent the unborn; the French system represents only those who vote, who are the machine's beneficiaries (F070?).

facts.statement: Two canonical results ground the complementarity argument: Kremer's O-ring theory (QJE 108(3), 1993) - production is chains of complementary tasks where one failing link destroys the value of all others; and Baumol's cost disease (Baumol & Bowen 1966; Baumol 2012, 'The Cost Disease', Yale UP) - as frontier productivity rises, the relative cost of labor-intensive essential services (care, teaching) rises mechanically, so the floor's affordability is funded by frontier growth or not at all.
facts.notes: Citations verified run 12.

facts.statement: France created a sovereign pension reserve fund (FRR) in 1999 to pre-fund the baby-boom retirement wave, then raided it a decade later: the 2010 pension reform (LFSS 2011) ordered the FRR to pay EUR 2.1bn per year to the social-debt amortization fund (CADES) from 2011 to 2024 (EUR 29.4bn in total) and redirected its revenue streams; payments of EUR 1.45bn/yr continue 2025-2033. The Cour des comptes called it 'the abandonment of a long-term ambition'.
facts.notes: Verified against Cour des comptes RPA 2011 and FRR annual report 2010. Resolves the FRR half of Q19. Load-bearing for III.12 (anti-capture design): the precedent proves the raid risk is not hypothetical - the essay's 'created a reserve fund and raided it a decade later' line now has its primary source.

facts.statement: The pen has already moved a knuckle: the EU Council placed France under an excessive deficit procedure on 26 July 2024; on 21 January 2025 the Council approved France's 2025-2029 medium-term plan with a seven-year adjustment path capping net primary expenditure growth (~1.1-1.2%/yr) to bring the deficit under 3% of GDP by 2029. French budgets are now negotiated under Brussels surveillance with annual progress reports.
facts.notes: Verified against EUR-Lex (COM(2024)716, Council rec.) and DG Tresor annual progress report (April 2026). For I.5/II.1: the 'who holds the pen' question is not hypothetical - a polite, weak version of the program already exists; the essay's point is that its logic strengthens with every downgrade.

facts.statement: The inflation exit is largely closed to France: about 11% of the state's negotiable debt (EUR 307bn of EUR 2,737bn, end-2025) is inflation-indexed and reprices immediately with inflation; the average maturity of the debt is ~8.5 years, so higher inflation feeds into rates on the ~EUR 300bn refinanced annually; pensions and the minimum wage are legally indexed to inflation, so spending reflates alongside. The 2021-2023 inflation surprise ran the natural experiment: the debt ratio fell ~5 points (from ~115% of GDP in 2020 to ~110% in 2023) then resumed climbing to 115.6% by 2025 because the primary deficit persisted.
facts.notes: AFT bulletin April 2026 (end-2025 stock and maturity data verified). The 2020-2023 debt-ratio dip values are from INSEE/Eurostat Maastricht series (F002's source); exact dip values (114.6->109.9) to pin if the essay quotes them. Grounds the new objection IV.15: inflation is a one-off levy the machine re-spends, not a policy.

facts.statement: The French pension system comprises 42 distinct affiliation situations (26 base regimes, 16 complementary, 3 additional - PLF 2025 'jaune' on public pensions); the Cour des comptes describes 'around forty distinct regimes' with partly specific rules. The commonly cited 'forty-two regimes' is accurate as affiliation situations.
facts.notes: Verified against the PLF 2025 jaune budgetaire and Cour des comptes (Feb 2025). Supports the essay's 'one points-based system replaces the forty-two existing regimes' line.

facts.statement: The mean-vs-median caveat, pinned: on the OECD Income Distribution Database (2023, converted at the OECD's household-consumption PPPs), median equivalised disposable income is $38,752 (France) vs $49,885 (US) - France at 77.7% of the US median, a 22.3% gap; the same dataset's MEAN gap is 28.1%. LIS (2022, int-$ 2021 prices) gives a 25.6% median gap. The median gap runs 5-6 points below the mean gap in every year of both series. The honest prose rendering: 'a third behind at the average, roughly a quarter median to median'.
facts.notes: Verified run 14 [Q34 resolved]. Honesty in both directions: (a) cash disposable income omits in-kind transfers (worth >30% of French disposable income per OECD WP 130 [S091]; 51% of France's broadened inequality reduction per INSEE Analyses 118 [S090]) and omits US out-of-pocket health costs (~$9,860/yr premiums+cost-sharing for an insured family of four, KFF 2024 [S089]) - so the median comparison understates France; (b) even the OECD measure that ADDS in-kind services back (How's Life adjusted disposable income, 2023: $48,534 vs $64,233) leaves the US mean ~24% ahead - the caveats shave the gap, they do not erase it. VINTAGE WARNING: the median gap was 31-32% in 2019-2021; the narrowing to ~22-26% is recent and partly an artifact of expiring US pandemic transfers and the ICP-2021 PPP re-benchmarking. Never write 'the gap collapses at the median'. The BdF 33% (constant 2015 PPPs) and the current-PPP ~26% GDP gap are different vintages of the same yardstick [F006 notes].

facts.statement: French retirees' standard of living, measured: in cash terms they match the whole population (2022: median 100%, EUR 2,030/month; mean 97%); counting imputed rents (they mostly own homes outright) they live ABOVE it - +5 to +6.5% on COR's mean measure (106.5% per COR Feb 2026), +9.5% on DREES's median measure (2019). Retiree poverty: 10.0% vs 14.4% whole population (2022); on the OECD definition, French 65+ poverty (6.1%) is less than half the OECD average (14.8%). OECD comparison: French 65+ income = 94.3% of population income (2022 incomes, 11th of 37; ~99.8% and top-3 on the 2020-income vintage - the 2022 dip is the inflation year). Net pension replacement rate 70.0% vs OECD 63.2%; public pension spending 4th in the OECD (after Greece, Italy, Austria). COR projects the ratio falling to ~90% by 2070 under current law.
facts.notes: Verified run 13. PRECISION DISCIPLINE: 'retirees live better than workers' is true only WITH imputed rents; in cash terms it is parity (and mean 3% below in the 2022 inflation year). The essay says 'as well as, and counting their mortgage-free homes, better'. Also record the perception gap (COR Feb 2026): 49% of French believe retirees live WORSE than the population; 20% better.

facts.statement: The old hold the capital, and the transfer overshoots consumption: households aged 50-79 hold 61% of French gross household wealth while being 50% of households (INSEE HVP 2024); retired households' mean NET wealth is EUR 310,000 vs 240,000 for working households (+29%, COR/HVP 2021). The 60+ share of wealth rose from 36% to 45.5% over 2004-2014 alone (Arrondel-Masson); in 1986 the median net wealth of the 70+ was one-third that of the 50-59, today it is comparable, while the under-40s' median halved relative to the 50-59 (France Strategie). Homeownership: 17% of under-30 households vs 71-76% at 70+, generally mortgage-free from 65. And retirees keep saving: net saving rate ~8% at 65+, and 65+ households contributed about two-thirds of the 2023-24 rise in the national saving rate (COR).
facts.notes: Verified run 13. The saving-rate fact is the sharpest: a pay-as-you-go transfer exists to fund old-age consumption; when its recipients save 8% of income as a group, the transfer exceeds need at the margin by construction. Caveats: survey wealth data truncates the very top and excludes institutionalized households; the 61% figure is gross wealth.

facts.statement: Inheritance arrives too late to capitalize the young: the average French heir is ~50 years old (vs ~30 in 1900), heading to 58 by 2050 (France Strategie/CAE). Inherited wealth has risen from ~35% of total wealth in the early 1970s to ~60% today (CAE 2021). Concentration: half of French people inherit less than EUR 70,000 over a lifetime; fewer than 10% inherit more than 500,000; the top 1% of heirs receives on average over EUR 4.2mn net of duties (~180x the median for the top 0.1%, vs ~10x for the equivalent labor-income ratio).
facts.notes: Verified run 13 (CAE note 69; France Strategie NA 51). ~40% of transmitted wealth escapes fiscal succession data (assurance-vie, dismemberment, Dutreil) - these are reconstructed lifetime-flow estimates. Wealth flows old-to-almost-old: with heirs at 50+, bequests recycle wealth within the older half of the distribution.

facts.statement: The 10% pension abattement (art. 158-5-a CGI): retirees deduct 10% of pensions from taxable income, mirroring the wage earners' 10% deduction for professional expenses - expenses pensions do not carry. Created by amendment in the 1978 budget (Papon, rapporteur general) AGAINST the government: budget minister Robert Boulin objected in session (18 Oct 1977) that retirees' costs 'are not professional expenses'; parliament passed it and made it permanent. Cost: EUR 4.5-4.8bn/yr (PLF 2024/2026 vintages), 14.8mn beneficiary households, ~30% of the benefit to the top income decile; caps: EUR 4,399 per retired HOUSEHOLD vs EUR 14,426 per WORKING PERSON (2024 incomes). The CPO recommended abolition (Oct 2024). PLF 2026 tested the impasse: the government proposed replacing it with a flat EUR 2,000 per pensioner (yield ~1.2bn); the Assemblee nationale deleted the reform on 13 Nov 2025 by 213 votes to 17; the adopted budget (loi 2026-103, 19 Feb 2026) keeps the abattement intact, indexed.
facts.notes: Verified run 13 (CPO note Oct 2024 incl. the 1977 travaux; LF 2026 outcome). The 1977 origin story is the fingerprint in its purest form: the executive said the deduction had no rationale; the elected chamber created it anyway, and defended it 213-17 forty-eight years later. Honest caveat: the original 1977 rationale (smoothing the income drop at retirement before withholding-at-source) existed but the CPO judges it void since 2019 withholding.

facts.statement: The indexation asymmetry is a DEFAULT-RULE asymmetry: pensions rise with inflation automatically by statute (art. L161-25 CSS; the coefficient cannot go below 1, so no nominal cuts; freezing requires an affirmative vote deputies must own), while the income-tax bareme is indexed only if each year's budget affirmatively votes it. Recent record: +5.3% (Jan 2024), +2.2% (Jan 2025), +0.9% (Jan 2026). Both attempted squeezes died: Barnier's 6-month indexation delay fell with his government (Dec 2024); Bayrou's 'annee blanche' (July 2025) was stripped from the budget twice and the LFSS 2026 passed without it. December 2024 demonstrated both defaults in one stroke: the censure killed the budget, so pensions got the full +2.2% automatically while income-tax brackets stayed frozen until the LF 2025 passed in mid-February. Meanwhile the ceilings of workers' wealth-building vehicles sit unindexed for decades: PEA EUR 150,000 since 2014, assurance-vie abattements EUR 152,500 / 4,600-9,200 since 1998, Livret A EUR 22,950 since 2013.
facts.notes: Verified run 13. HONESTY: (1) the bareme IS normally indexed each year (exception: the 2012-2013 freeze, which hit everyone); the asymmetry is who bears the burden of inaction; (2) the frozen savings ceilings are age-neutral instruments (holdings skew old) - weak evidence of pro-retiree INTENT on their own; the strong contrast is statutory pension indexation vs everything else discretionary. The essay leans on the default-rule contrast and December 2024, not on the PEA/AV freezes.

facts.statement: The CSG asymmetry and the 2018-2019 natural experiment: CSG runs at 9.2% on wages vs 8.3% maximum on pensions (with reduced bands 6.6%/3.8%/0% - only ~29% of retirees pay the top rate). The 2018 CSG hike (+1.7pp) was over-compensated for workers by abolishing their sickness and unemployment contributions, while retirees bore it raw - the one recent attempt to shift net burden onto pensions. Within twelve months (loi MUES, 24 Dec 2018, after the gilets jaunes), the hike was repealed for pensions under ~EUR 2,000/month: 3.8 million households, roughly 70% of retirees restored.
facts.notes: Verified run 13. Caveat: the reversal's proximate trigger was a street movement, not an election; and the top ~29% of pensions kept the hike. Still: burden shifted onto workers sticks; burden shifted onto retirees lasted a year.

facts.statement: On 4 December 2024, the Assemblee nationale censured the Barnier government (331 votes; first successful censure since October 1962) over the PLFSS 2025 - whose pension under-indexation was the pivot group's declared 'absolute red line' (RN). The fallen budget meant the statutory default applied: all pensions were revalorized the full +2.2% on 1 January 2025. Partly, a French government fell over trying to under-index pensions, and the pensions won.
facts.notes: Verified run 13. Caveat kept sharp: the censure motion was the left's and carried broader grievances; pension indexation was the RN's explicit condition, not the sole cause. 'Partly over pension indexation' is the honest phrasing; 'over pension indexation' alone overstates.

facts.statement: The counterevidence, recorded: majority governments DID squeeze pensions repeatedly - the 2014 law shifted revalorization by six months; 2018 skipped a year entirely; 2019 and 2020 capped revalorization at +0.3% against ~1.8% inflation; the 2014 budget fiscalized the 10% family pension bonus (EUR 1.2bn/yr) and it stayed fiscalized. The refined claim the full record supports: touching retirees is survivable for a government with a majority and fatal without one. Since the assembly hung in 2022, every attempt has died: the indexation delay brought down a government (Dec 2024), the 'annee blanche' was stripped twice (2025), the abattement reform lost 213-17 (Nov 2025).
facts.notes: Verified run 13. This SHARPENS C25 rather than weakening it: the electoral constraint binds exactly when the median voter's proxies hold the parliamentary balance - which demography makes more likely every cycle [F070][F038].

facts.statement: The Greek forced adjustment did not pick its victims by tax tables. The DESIGNED measures were broadly progressive on paper: holding 2009 deciles fixed, the poorest 10% lost 34% of income by 2013 against a 36% average (public-wage cuts drove the progressivity; VAT hikes were the regressive exception). The collapse around the measures created a new poor: re-ranked, the income of whoever occupied the bottom decile in 2013 was 69% below its 2009 counterpart (twice the average loss); ~65% of the population changed decile 2009-2013; at-risk-of-poverty ANCHORED at 2008 rose from 18.0% (2010) to 44.3% (2013) and 48.0% (2014-2015). Austerity's first-order effects account for roughly half of the anchored-poverty rise in 2010-11 and a third in 2013; the rest arrived through mass unemployment.
facts.notes: Verified run 14 [Q20 resolved]. CORRECTS the essay's earlier line 'the poorest quarter pays fastest' - wrong as written: the mechanism was mass unemployment plus a safety net with no minimum-income floor for the new poor, NOT regressive tax-benefit design. Never blur designed-progressivity with outcome-regressivity in prose. The 13.2->27.4% anchored series in S085 uses a different anchor; do not mix the two series - the essay quotes Eurostat ilc_li22b (18->48).

facts.statement: The Greek adjustment's generational incidence: youth (15-24) unemployment 59.2% annual in 2013 (monthly peak 61.4% mid-2013), above 50% for four consecutive years (2012-2015). Relative poverty for 65+ FELL from 21.3% (2010) to 13.7% (2015) while for 18-24 it rose from 22.3% (2009) to 34.1% (2013); anchored poverty rose +32.4pp for ages 18-29 vs +20.4pp for 65+ (2009-2013); the elderly's share of the bottom quintile halved (18% to 10%). About 427,000 residents aged 15-64 left Greece over 2008-2013/14, ~223,000 of them aged 25-39, disproportionately educated (Bank of Greece). Pensions in payment were cut on 10-12 occasions, cumulatively ~14% (smallest pensions) to 40-50% (largest), progressive by design: pensioners were relatively, not absolutely, protected (their anchored poverty still reached ~47% by 2014).
facts.notes: Verified run 14 [Q20 resolved]. The load-bearing symmetry for C14/C25: the forced adjustment reproduced the insider/outsider machine - the settled kept their relative place, the young and the newly unemployed absorbed the collapse. 'Sixty percent youth unemployment' in prose = 59.2 annual / 61.4 monthly peak, fair rounding.

facts.statement: What a forced consolidation cuts first: Greek general government investment fell from ~EUR 14bn (2009) to under EUR 5bn (2011) and stayed there through the third program, against a first-program plan of only ~0.2pp of GDP - peer-reviewed work calls public investment the 'flagship adjustment variable' because it is politically the easiest line to cut. The IMF's own ex-post evaluation of the 2010 SBA concedes on the record: growth projections were far too optimistic, an upfront debt restructuring 'would have been better for Greece' but was unacceptable to euro partners, and the lesson is 'the importance of spreading the burden of adjustment across different strata of society' (the 2016 background paper glosses: the burden 'was not sufficiently spread').
facts.notes: Verified run 14 [Q20 resolved]. 'Fell by two thirds in two years' is the honest prose rendering (14 -> <5).

facts.statement: Euro exit is not legally impossible: essentially all French negotiable government debt is issued under French law (foreign-law international bonds of the French general government are ~zero on BIS data), so parliament could redenominate by lex monetae. The euro-CACs mandatory on all euro-area issues since 2013 (~83% of the OAT stock by end-Sept 2025 on AFT bond-by-bond data) do not block a statutory currency change on the dominant legal-economic view (De Santis/ECB via CEPR; Codogno & Galli), though litigation would be certain.
facts.notes: Recorded deliberately so the essay never overclaims legal impossibility: the answer to the euro-exit objection must rest on economics, not law.

facts.statement: The costed economics of a franc return: redenominating French-law debt into a depreciating franc is a default under S&P's and Moody's published definitions (both said so publicly in Feb 2017 about the FN plan) and a Restructuring credit event under ISDA's 2014 CDS definitions. The FN's own experts assumed a new-franc depreciation 'on the order of 20%'; Institut Montaigne's costing (liberal-leaning, flagged) put the median scenario at -2.3% GDP in year one (range -0.6 to -3.2), ~-9% long run, ~500,000 jobs destroyed; OFCE's equilibrium estimate of the franc's needed real depreciation is ~11%, and OFCE and CEPII both concluded the competitiveness gain would net to about zero (southern members would exit and depreciate alongside) while the dominant effect is a balance-sheet banking crisis. Compiled Grexit estimates (IMF, NBG, Citigroup, BNP) ran -13% to -22% of GDP for the exiting debtor.
facts.notes: Direction uncontested across sources of three different leanings (Montaigne liberal, OFCE Keynesian-left, CEPII public); magnitudes are scenario estimates, confidence medium on any single number, high on the sign and order of magnitude. Grexit numbers are for Greece, a smaller and already-broken economy: use only as the family of estimates, never as a French forecast.

facts.statement: Greece 2015, the dress rehearsal inside the euro: EUR 47.6bn of deposits (27.5% of the deposit base) left Greek banks between December 2014 and 28 June 2015 on the mere possibility of exit; capital controls were imposed by legislative act on 28 June 2015; banks stayed closed for three weeks (reopened 20 July); ATM withdrawals were capped at EUR 60 per day per card; controls were fully lifted only in September 2019.
facts.notes: Verified run 14. The strongest single exhibit for the euro-exit objection: this is what the approach to the door cost a country that stayed inside.

facts.statement: What printing francs cannot buy: France's net energy import bill was EUR 116.3bn in 2022 (record year; oil and biofuels 58.6, natural gas 46.7 - essentially dollar-priced fossil imports), ~EUR 71bn in 2023, ~EUR 56-58bn in 2024 (provisional, SDES). France runs a structural current-account deficit, and the Banque de France's TARGET2 position is a net liability oscillating roughly between -EUR 110bn and -EUR 240bn through 2024-25, which on exit would fall due in euros.
facts.notes: TARGET2 single-month figures are volatile; verify on the ECB statistics page before quoting any one month. The essay quotes only the 2022 energy bill.

facts.statement: The political record of euro exit: both French parties that carried the proposal dropped it. The RN declared exit 'no longer a priority' (Jan 2019) and formally abandoned the franc in its April 2019 European manifesto; reporting at the time attributed the reversal to the proposal terrifying retirees, the wealth-holding cohort. LFI replaced its 2017 'plan B' with 'disobedience' in the 2021 edition of L'Avenir en commun and signed 'ni quitter l'Europe ni quitter l'euro' into the 2022 NUPES accord; Melenchon cited the external deficit ('I don't see how we would manage, given our external trade deficit', Jan 2022, translated). Opinion: euro-area support for the euro hit a record 83% (Eurobarometer 103, spring 2025); France is the euro area's lowest-support member; Cluster17 (Sept 2025): 59% of French prefer the euro, 23% a national currency.
facts.notes: High confidence on the party record (multiple press-of-record accounts, platform texts); medium on the single-wave Cluster17 split; the retiree attribution for the RN reversal is the press's interpretation and must stay attributed in prose. Melenchon's stated reason is the thesis's own argument from its opponent's mouth - see F078 for why retirees' balance sheets decide this. Exact French Eurobarometer percentage still unpinned [Q35].

facts.statement: The lump-of-labor refutation, canonical: the NBER twelve-country study (Gruber-Wise 2010) found 'no evidence that increasing the labor force participation of older persons reduces the job opportunities of young persons. Indeed, the evidence suggests that greater labor force participation of older persons is associated with greater youth employment and with reduced youth unemployment.' Pooled panel estimates (country+year fixed effects): +1pp employment of the 55-64 is associated with +0.54 to +0.91pp YOUTH employment; every statistically significant estimate on youth unemployment is negative. Germany's 1972 natural experiment: senior employment -7pp in four years, youth employment FELL 2pp, youth unemployment ROSE 1.7pp.
facts.notes: Read directly from the published introduction (Gruber, Milligan, Wise). Method: within-country natural experiments + cross-country + panel regressions, all same sign. The term 'lump of labour' fallacy dates to D.F. Schloss, The Economic Review, 1891.

facts.statement: France ran the lump-of-labor experiment at full scale and billed it as job liberation: PM Pierre Mauroy (Lille, 27 Sept 1981): the oldest should 'release jobs so that everyone can have a job'; the 1977 GRD agreement preamble promised 'the release of jobs allowing many unemployed to find jobs'; contrats de solidarite triggered ~200,000 early departures in 1982-83 alone; retirement moved to 60 in 1983. Employment of French 55-64s fell ~21pp between 1971 and 1993 (60-64 employment: >55% in 1975 to 16.5% in 1995). Youth unemployment over the same arc: 6% (end-1973) to 14% (end-1980) to 25% (end-1984); the under-25 rate has never returned below 15% since 1982. When senior employment recovered (1993-2005, and again 2013-2023: 55-64 rate ~47% to ~58%), youth employment rose and youth unemployment fell (25% peak 2013 to ~17% 2023).
facts.notes: Mauroy and ministry quotes cited in the Gruber-Wise volume (from Gaullier 1982 and Droit social, April 1983). The France chapter (Ben Salem-Blanchet-Bozio-Roger, LFS 1968-2005): higher senior participation correlates with HIGHER youth employment, controlling for cycle; authors' honest caveat recorded (incentives were endogenous to rising unemployment; single-country causal identification is hard - the cross-country evidence in F093 carries the causal weight). Correlation-vs-causation discipline: the 1971-93 arc is an illustration, not an estimate.

facts.statement: The senior-employment / youth-unemployment cross-section runs against the lump of labor everywhere (2024, OECD): Japan 79.2% senior (55-64) employment / 4.0% youth (15-24) unemployment; Iceland 80.9/9.1; Germany 75.0/6.7; Switzerland 75.1/8.2 - versus France 60.4/18.7; Italy 59.0/20.3; Spain 61.1/26.5; Greece 57.3/22.4; Belgium 59.4/17.3.
facts.notes: OECD Infra-Annual Labour Statistics via FRED, annual 2024. Caveats: Sweden breaks the pattern (78.1/24.2 - largely a measurement artifact: full-time students seeking side jobs count as unemployed; never use Sweden here without the caveat). OECD dataset gives France 60.4/Germany 75.0 vs the Eurostat-based F011 (61.7/75.3) - different datasets, keep each internally consistent. Cross-section is illustrative; causal weight sits on F093/F094. CAE Note 32 (2016) is the citable French institutional rejection of job-freeing reasoning.

facts.statement: The honest counterevidence on raising retirement ages, recorded: (a) France's 2010 reform (60 to 62; Rabate-Rochut 2020, CNAV data): at age 60, employment +21pp but unemployment +13-14pp, disability +5.9pp, sickness +1.4pp - about one fifth of the pension savings leaked to other benefit schemes; the substitution hits the SENIORS themselves, not the young. (b) Firm-level displacement evidence is split: Boeri-Garibaldi-Moen (CEPR 2016) estimate Italy's 2011 Fornero reform cost ~36,000 youth hires in affected firms mid-recession; Carta-D'Amuri-von Wachter (NBER WP 28407), same reform, cleaner instrument: +10% older workers RAISED young employment 1.8% within firms, value added up proportionally. No French study attributes any rise in youth unemployment to the 2010 reform.
facts.notes: Design instruction, not rebuttal: the age lever works but leaks ~a fifth without senior-employability policy (health at work, retraining, hiring incentives 55+); the essay must pair the lever with that policy rather than claim frictionless transition. The firm-level split does not overturn the aggregate result (F093).

facts.statement: The Germany floor check, resolved (follows the data, corrects F056): on Eurostat SILC 2024 (income year 2023, PPS per equivalised person), Germany's floor is nominally ABOVE France's: P10 cutoff DE 13,066 vs FR 12,076 (+8%); P5 DE 10,555 vs FR 9,575 (+10%); at-risk-of-poverty rates a statistical tie (FR 15.9% vs DE 15.5%; severe material and social deprivation 6.6 vs 6.2). France led every year 2008-2016 (P10 2014: FR 10,611 vs DE 9,402, a 13% French lead); Germany crossed over by 2018-19, before its 2020 survey break. France keeps three narrower edges: housing (bottom-quintile housing-cost overburden FR 25.2% vs DE 33.3%; poor households' housing share 38.6% vs 43.8% - netting housing out brings the two floors back to parity, France marginally ahead); poverty depth (median poverty gap 18.8% vs 20.4%); and the OECD IDD's SOEP-based alternative reading (poverty at 50% line, 2023: FR 8.7% vs DE 11.3%) - the FR-DE poverty RANKING depends on which German survey one believes.
facts.notes: Q25's load-bearing half, resolved run 15. The claim 'France beats Germany at the floor today' is DEAD as a gross-income claim; the honest version: France's floor led by 13% as late as 2014, Germany caught up in the late 2010s while France stood still, and only France's cheaper housing keeps parity. Crossover predates the German survey break (not an artifact). Life-expectancy-by-income gaps are NOT comparable across the two countries (INSEE's 13-year gap uses 5% tails; the German RKI 8.6-year figure uses broad income bands - never print them side by side) [S115].

facts.statement: Germany's bottom decile stagnated through the Hartz era and was repaired by the minimum wage, not by growth alone: real net household income of the bottom decile in 2021 stood AT ITS 1995 LEVEL while the top decile gained 58% and the average 35% (DIW/SOEP 2025); real gross hourly wages in the bottom wage decile fell more than 25% between 1995 and 2005, converging back only after 2013, driven by the 2015 statutory minimum wage and its increases.
facts.notes: Two-edged and the thesis must keep both edges: (a) kills 'Germany shows growth alone lifts the bottom' - the Hartz-era bottom was squeezed, and the repair instrument was redistributive (minimum wage); (b) also kills complacency about the French floor - a Germany that squeezed its bottom for 20 years still caught up with a France that stood still on borrowed money (F097). Supports C19's two-curves frame: the floor needs growth AND design.

facts.statement: The US floor is below the French floor even though the US median is far above: OECD IDD 2023 (consumption PPPs), median equivalised disposable income US $49,885 vs FR $38,752 (US +29%); derived P10 (median divided by the published P50/P10 ratio): US ~$18,270 vs FR ~$20,180 - the poorest tenth of Americans are roughly 10% POORER than the poorest tenth of the French. Germany's derived P10 ~$20,500.
facts.notes: The P10 levels are a DERIVATION (published median / published P50-P10 ratio, both high-confidence), not a published statistic - print the qualitative form ('the poorest tenth of Americans are poorer than the poorest tenth of the French'), not the dollar figures. Direction consistent with the LIS-based literature and with F054 (mortality gradient). Pairs with F076 (median gap ~a quarter) as the complete mean/median/floor picture of the US comparison.

facts.statement: Decoupling speed, the honest numbers [Q31 resolved]: France's consumption-based CO2 fell 25.3% over 2005-2023 (-1.61%/yr) while real GDP grew 21.8% (+1.10%/yr) - absolute decoupling at ~-2.7%/yr intensity; in Vogel-Hickel's own 2013-19 window France achieved -1.5%/yr, almost exactly their 11-country average (1.6%/yr). Required rates: UNEP Emissions Gap 2024 says global GHG must fall 7.5%/yr for 1.5C and 4%/yr for 2C; Vogel-Hickel 2023: high-income countries' decoupling must accelerate ~10x by 2025 for 1.5C fair-shares; Hickel-Kallis 2020: without BECCS, global emissions must fall 6.8%/yr (1.5C) / 4%/yr (2C). France's own SNBC-3 requires ~-5%/yr to 2030; achieved: -6.8% in 2023 (one Paris-pace year), -1.8 to -3.0% in 2024 (vintage-dependent), ~-2% provisional 2025; the HCC says the 2024 pace must be multiplied by 2.3.
facts.notes: THE CONCESSION IS MANDATORY: France's observed record confirms the 'too slow' objection (one-fifth of the required 1.5C pace), it does not refute it. Never print the 2005-2023 record as an answer to the speed argument. GCP consumption series is CO2-only, excl. LULUCF and int'l bunkers; the all-GHG footprint (SDES) fell -1.7%/yr from 2010.
